archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (possession-first)
archetype.definition: Pittsburgh controls 5-on-5 play like a middle-of-the-pack team, but cold finishing, a weak power play and bad luck in close games have left it with one of the league's worst records.

report.headline: A decent 5-on-5 team buried by cold percentages and close losses
report.take:
The 7-14-2 record and the 28th spot on the site's Teams tab describe a bad team. The underlying play doesn't. Pittsburgh owns 52.1% of the expected goals at 5-on-5 (12th) and 52% of the shot attempts (7th), and its penalty kill sits 9th at 82%. That is the profile of a team that should be hovering around .500. Instead it is last in the Metropolitan, behind every team in the division including Columbus.

The gap comes from three places. The first is a 5-on-5 PDO of 96.9: neither the shooters nor the goalies are converting what the process generates. The second is Pts vs Goal Diff at -5.2, 30th in the league. Even a -14 goal differential should have produced more standings points than 16. The third is a power play at 18.8%, 27th and well below the league's 22.5%. That one carries real weight, because last season's unit ran at 24.1% and the offense ranked 3rd. This year the offense ranks 23rd while the 5-on-5 process has held up, with xGF % even a touch better than last year's 51%. The shots are coming at about the same quality. They aren't going in.

None of this makes the last month harmless. November went 2-7, and over the last five games the team scored 1.8 goals a game, down 1.11 on its season rate. The losses included 3-4 at Nashville and 0-1 at Dallas, along with 4-5 in Montreal and 2-3 to Vegas just before that. Those are the losses a regressing shooting percentage turns into points. The goaltending is a real but secondary problem. Arturs Silovs is at .878 and Sergei Murashov at .891, both with negative GSAx, which earns the group a C-. The blueline grades F, and the one listed defenseman, Trevor van Riemsdyk, sits 36th of 36 on his tab.

The outlook is better than the standings suggest but not good. Percentages like these usually drift back toward normal, and the Penguins should play closer to .500 hockey the rest of the way. The hole is deep, though: a 57-point pace and 59 games left. A playoff push needs both the power play and the goaltending to turn, not just the bounces.

strengths.title: Winning the 5-on-5 territory battle
strengths.body: Pittsburgh carries 52% of the shot attempts (7th) and 52.1% of the expected goals (12th), both above the league's average. That fits the club's recent history: CF % has sat at .50-.52 for five straight seasons, so this is a stable trait rather than a hot streak. It is the main reason to expect the record to improve.

strengths.title: A penalty kill that holds up
strengths.body: At 82%, the kill ranks 9th and runs well above the league's 77.2%. That is better than any season since 2021-22. It has kept the special-teams damage one-sided rather than total, and a kill built on structure tends to hold better than shooting luck does.

concerns.title: Finishing and the power play dried up
concerns.body: The offense fell from 3rd last season to 23rd now, and the last five games produced 1.8 goals a game. The 5-on-5 chances haven't disappeared, so most of the drop is conversion. The power play is part of the story too, at 18.8% against last year's 24.1%. Shooting luck should come back; the power play is less certain.

concerns.title: Goaltending below average, blueline worse
concerns.body: Neither goalie is saving what an average goalie would: Silovs is at .878 with -1.4 GSAx and Murashov at .891 with -2. The group grades C-, and the blueline grades F. The defense is also giving up the second-most points to opposing centers relative to expectation, ranking 31st. Opponents getting 28 shots a game is slightly worse than the league, so the goalies aren't drowning, but they aren't bailing anyone out either.

concerns.title: Close games keep going the wrong way
concerns.body: Pts vs Goal Diff of -5.2 ranks 30th: the team has fewer points than its goal margin implies. The recent run of one-goal losses at Nashville, Dallas, Montreal and against Vegas shows it. Mostly this is noise that should even out, but the 16 points are already banked short.

trend.note: A 4-9 October slid into a 2-7 November, and the last ten games went 2-8-0 with scoring dropping hardest in the last five. The underlying 5-on-5 numbers haven't fallen with it, so the slide is mostly about results, not play.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games against weak-process teams: a chance to stop the bleeding
weekAhead.body:
Calgary, Buffalo, Toronto and Columbus all sit above Pittsburgh on the site's Teams tab, but none of them out-chances opponents. Their xGF % shares rank 24th, 20th, 26th and 22nd, all below Pittsburgh's 12th. Three of the four games are at home. If the Penguins' process holds, this is the softest-looking stretch of the season by quality of play.

The opponents' goaltending helps too. Calgary's goalies grade D-, Buffalo's D+ with a .879 save percentage (27th), and Toronto's goalies are at -5.2 GSAx. For a team whose problem is finishing, these are the nets where the percentages should start to turn. Columbus is the exception: its goaltending is near average and it is 4th at holding forwards under expectation.

keyMatchups.title: Power play against Buffalo's leaky kill
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo kills only 72.3% of penalties (26th), the best chance all week for a 27th-ranked power play to find a rhythm. A goal or two with the man advantage in Buffalo would mean more than any single result.

keyMatchups.title: Penalty kill against Calgary's power play
keyMatchups.body: Calgary scores on 26.3% of its power plays (5th), and its 3.1 Pts vs Goal Diff shows a team winning close games it probably shouldn't. Pittsburgh's 9th-ranked kill has to neutralize that, because at 5-on-5 the Flames sit 24th in xGF %.

keyMatchups.title: Toronto, a mirror image with worse play
keyMatchups.body: Toronto shares Pittsburgh's -5.2 Pts vs Goal Diff, but it gets out-chanced at 46.1% xGF and allows 28.8 shots a game (25th). At home, this is the game the Penguins' 5-on-5 edge should decide.

weekAhead.watch: Whether the Penguins get back above two goals a game against Buffalo's and Calgary's below-par goaltending. If the scoring doesn't come against these goalies, the finishing problem is more than bad luck.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect improvement but not rescue. The 5-on-5 shares and the penalty kill point to a team that plays like a fringe .500 club. A 96.9 PDO and a -5.2 Pts vs Goal Diff are the kinds of numbers that usually even out over 59 games. Our estimate is roughly 25-28 more wins, for 32-35 total, and somewhere in the low-to-mid 70s in standings points: well above the current 57-point pace, but short of what a playoff spot requires.

What won't simply regress is the goaltending and the power play. Both goalies are below expected, and the power play has fallen from last year's level without an obvious luck explanation. If either recovers to last season's form, the upper end of these ranges is in play. If neither does, the possession edge will keep producing respectable games and too many one-goal losses.

projections.stat: Goals scored / game, rest of season

swingFactors: Silovs and Murashov getting back toward average save percentages
Power play recovering toward last season's 24.1%
Shooting luck turning so the 5-on-5 edge becomes goals

confidence.note: 23 games is a real sample for shot shares but not for percentages; the forwards aren't listed and the all-situations shooting line looks incomplete.
